One fix, in the part of the extension that holds your Garmin password.

## The OS vault was reached on one platform only

The bundle carried a single native keytar binary — the one belonging to whichever
machine packed it. `npm install` builds or downloads that binary for the platform
doing the install, and a `.mcpb` is packed once and installed everywhere, so the
binary loaded on that one platform and nowhere else.

The consequence was quiet, because the extension is written to survive it: when
keytar cannot load, the encryption key goes to `.encryption.key` in the data
directory, owner-readable only, and everything keeps working. But it meant that
on Windows and macOS — where Claude Desktop runs — the key was not in the
Credential Manager or the Keychain, while the extension's own settings screen and
its privacy policy said it was.

The bundle now carries one binary per platform under `vendor/keytar`:

| Platform | Architectures |
|---|---|
| macOS | `x64`, `arm64` |
| Windows | `x64`, `ia32` |
| Linux | `x64`, `arm64` |

The server loads the one matching `process.platform` and `process.arch`. They are
fetched at pack time by keytar's own `prebuild-install`, so they are the same
artifacts npm would have downloaded on each platform.

Nothing changes for a clone of the repository: there, keytar is installed for the
machine it runs on and that copy is still preferred.

## The fallback is still there, and now documented

An architecture with no published prebuild, or a Linux session with no keyring
daemon running, still lands on the file-based key store. Credentials and tokens
are encrypted with AES-256-GCM either way; what differs is where the key that
decrypts them is kept. `check_credentials` reports which of the two is in use, and
the privacy policy now describes both instead of only the vault.

## Upgrading

Reinstall the bundle and restart Claude Desktop. Your credentials survive: an
existing install has its key in `.encryption.key`, and on the first start after the
upgrade the extension moves that key into the vault and deletes the file. If the
vault refuses — no keyring daemon, for instance — the key stays in the file and
nothing is lost; the move is attempted again on the next start.

The code to migrate a key had been in the project for some time but was never
called. It runs now.

## Install

Download `garmin-mcp-ts.mcpb` and open it with Claude Desktop, or drag it onto
Settings → Extensions. Verify the download first:

```
sha256sum -c garmin-mcp-ts.mcpb.sha256
```

**Full changelog**: https://github.com/sedoglia/garmin-mcp-ts/compare/v4.3.1...v4.3.2
